Introduction
Stability and appropriate load distribution in TKA are critical for successful long-term
outcomes. Biomechanical benefits of successful alignment include increased longevity of
the implants, achieved by avoiding wear and aseptic loosening. Successful alignment
results in decreased shear and mechanical stresses on implant/cement or cement/bone
interfaces and in decreased wear, deformation, and delamination of bearing surfaces
from eccentric or off-axis loading. Similarly, kinematic benefits of successful soft-tissue
balancing include proportional force transmission to ligamentous structures and the
soft-tissue envelope, thereby decreasing pain and stiffness; avoidance of unbalanced or
unstable gaps in flexion, midflexion, and extension, leading to greater stability during
gait; restoration of the full arc of motion to the knee; and proper tracking of the patella.
Alignment is not the only aspect of creating the perception of a normal knee because
implant design also plays an important role. For example, most TKA designs are deficient
at the anterior cruciate ligament and the medial meniscal ligament, both of which are
critical components of native knee kinematics. Newer implant designs and surgical
techniques aim to counter these deficiencies.
Fundamentals Radiographic Measurements
Coronal plane assessment using weight-bearing short- and long-leg radiographs
Alignment axes include mechanical, anatomic, and rotational axes (Figure 1).

Fundamentals Radiographic Measurements
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Alignment Strategies in Total Knee Arthroplasty

4/17

Coronal plane assessment using weight-bearing knee radiographs aids in preoperative
evaluation of disease and alignment. Long-leg AP radiographs are required to assess
alignment because short-leg radiographs are inadequate. In addition, supine
radiographs are insufficient to determine the severity of arthritis and overall alignment
of the knee.
Alignment axes include mechanical, anatomic, and rotational axes. The mechanical axis
of the lower extremity is determined by drawing a line from the center of the femoral
head to the center of the ankle and can be further subdivided into the mechanical axes
of the femur and tibia. The femoral mechanical axis is determined by drawing a line from
the center of the femoral head to the intercondylar notch. The tibial mechanical axis is
determined by drawing a line from the center of the proximal tibia to the center of the
talus. The tibial mechanical axis typically is in line with the anatomic axis of the tibia but
may vary on an AP radiograph with tibial bowing and rotation. The hip-knee-ankle (HKA)
angle is the medial angle formed between the femoral and tibial mechanical axes.
Perfect mechanical alignment requires the HKA angle to be 180°.
The anatomic axis of the lower extremity is determined by drawing a line in the middle
of the femoral and tibial intramedullary canal. The anatomic axis of the femur is
approximately 9° valgus, and the anatomic axis of the tibia is approximately 3° varus
relative to the mechanical axis. The anatomic femoral-tibial angle is the difference
between femoral anatomic alignment (9° valgus) and tibial anatomic alignment (3°
varus), which is a mean of 6° of valgus.
The rotational or kinematic axes of knee are the three functional rotational planes of
knee motion1: the transverse axis of the femur around which the tibia flexes and
extends, the transverse axis of the femur to which the patella flexes and extends, and
the longitudinal axis about which the tibia internally and externally rotates. The
transverse axis of femur around which the tibia flexes and extends passes through the
center of a circle that encompasses the cross-sectional radius of both femoral condyles.
This axis is not collinear to the transepicondylar axis. The transverse axis of the femur
around which the patella flexes and extends is located anterior and proximal to the first

approximately perpendicular to the first two axes.
Strategies for Alignment and Balancing in TKA
Mechanical Alignment
Mechanical alignment is the most commonly used alignment strategy.
It aims to align the centers of the hip, knee, and ankle of a patient in bipedal stance along a
straight line orthogonal to the floor, with the joint line parallel to the floor.
Mechanical alignment was designed to optimize the biomechanics of TKA to prevent the
aseptic loosening, polyethylene wear, and patellar instability associated with early implant
designs.
Mechanical alignment is achieved by setting the femoral joint line at 6° of valgus relative to
the femoral anatomic axis and the tibial joint line orthogonal to the tibial anatomic axis to
achieve a 180° HKA angle.
The femoral component rotation is externally rotated relative to the posterior condyle axis
by 3° to establish a rectangular flexion gap and adjust for the loss of tibial joint line varus.
If the gaps are not balanced at 0° and 90° of flexion, selective soft-tissue releases are
performed to create matched and balanced gaps.
The adoption of mechanical alignment leads, in part, to a marked improvement in implant
survivorship.2 Additional improvements are accrued via the adoption of more resistant
polyethylene, more forgiving implant design features, and more effective cementing
techniques.
Despite improvements in implant survival, by the early 2000s patient-reported outcome
measures suggested that 20% of patients were dissatisfied with TKA.3
Measured Resection Versus Balanced-Gap Mechanical Alignment
Techniques
Measured resection technique
The classic technique to achieve mechanical alignment without raising or lowering the joint
line (Video 1)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004027
6/17

After setting an intramedullary jig to between 5° and 7° of valgus relative to the femoral
anatomic axis, the maximum distal femur resection is set to match the thickness of the
femoral component, (generally 8 to 9 mm). This often leads to an asymmetric cut of the distal
femurs because the femoral anatomic axis is in a mean of 3° more valgus.
Similarly, the posterior condyle cuts are set to match the transepicondylar axis or 3° of
external rotation from the posterior condyle axis. The maximum resection is intended to
match the thickness of the posterior condyles of the femoral component (generally 8 to 9
mm), and the resections generally are asymmetric if the posterior condyle axis is not
collinear to the transepicondylar axis.
The tibial cut is independent of the femoral cuts and is set orthogonal to the anatomic axis of
the tibia while resecting an amount of bone equal to the thickness of the tibial tray plus the
thinnest liner available for that implant system. The cut bone often is trapezoidal if the joint
line orientation angle is not orthogonal to the tibial mechanical axis.
The rotation of the tibia is set to match native tibial rotation (various methods), and the slope
is orthogonal to the weight-bearing axis in posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)-sacrificing
designs or equal to the native slope if the PCL is retained.
Then soft-tissue balancing is performed by releasing structures, such as ligaments, tendons,
and capsule, from the tight side to create rectangular gaps in flexion and extension after the
removal of osteophytes.
Balanced-gap technique
Designed to minimize the number of soft-tissue releases required while achieving overall
mechanical alignment4,5 (Resources 1 and 2)
The balanced-gap technique involves tying the femoral component rotation to the tibial cut,
achieving a balanced gap in flexion without the need for additional releases. First, the tibia is
cut at 90° and then femoral component rotation is set in flexion parallel to the tibia with the
collateral ligaments under equal tension.
In patients with considerable preoperative so-called constitutional varus, surgeons may
choose to cut the tibia with up to 3° of varus. If femoral component rotation is set in flexion,
the rotation of the femoral cutting block will be closer to its normal posterior condyle axis (ie,
not externally rotated from its native rotation).
By setting femoral rotation to match the tibial cut during the balanced-gap technique, tissue
balancing in flexion and extension is achieved with fewer releases compared with the
mechanical alignment technique.

Measured Resection Versus Balanced-Gap Mechanical Alignment
Techniques
The most commonly used alignment strategy, mechanical alignment aims to align the
centers of the hip, knee, and ankle of a patient in bipedal stance along a straight line
orthogonal to the floor and the joint line parallel to the floor. Therefore, the HKA angle is
intended to be 180°. This alignment strategy was designed to optimize the biomechanics
of TKA to solve many problems associated with early TKA implants that often failed
because of aseptic loosening, polyethylene wear, mechanical failure of components, and
patellar instability.
To achieve mechanical alignment, the femoral joint line is set at 6° of valgus relative to
the femoral anatomic axis and the tibial joint line is set orthogonal to the tibial anatomic
axis to achieve a 180° HKA angle. The femoral component is externally rotated relative to

the posterior condyle axis by 3° to establish a rectangular flexion gap and adjust for the
loss of tibial joint line varus. If the gaps are not balanced, selective soft-tissue releases
are performed. The goal is to achieve matched and balanced gaps in flexion and
extension.
By aligning the hip, knee, and ankle along a fixed, neutral axis, mechanical alignment
principles in combination with soft-tissue releases ensure direct axial loading of the
implants and balanced gaps in full extension and at 90° of flexion. Mechanical alignment
resulted in, at least in part, a marked improvement in implant survivorship.2 Additional
improvements accrued via the adoption of more resistant polyethylene, more forgiving
implant design features, and more effective cementing technique. Despite
improvements in implant survival, by the early 2000s patient-reported outcome
measures suggested that 20% of patients were dissatisfied with TKA.3
Robotics, navigation, and advanced alignment techniques increased the surgical
accuracy of mechanical alignment; however, functional outcomes in terms of patient
satisfaction have not been shown to change.6 Although mechanical alignment achieves
clear biomechanical benefits, the challenges associated with soft-tissue balancing and
restoring normal kinematics via this technique recently have been underscored with the
use of intraoperative sensor measurements, showing that mechanical alignment
restores normal compartment pressures in fewer than 30% to 40% of patients. Recent
data confirm that 10% to 20% of patients who undergo mechanical alignment are not
completely satisfied after TKA.7,8
Two different surgical techniques that can be used to achieve mechanical alignment are
the measured resection technique and the balanced-gap technique. Measured resection
is the classic technique to achieve mechanical alignment without raising or lowering the
joint line (Video 1). After setting an intramedullary jig to between 5° and 7° of valgus
relative to the femoral anatomic axis, the maximum distal femur resection is set to
match the thickness of the femoral component, generally 8 to 9 mm. Frequently, this
results in asymmetric resection of bone from the medial and lateral femoral condyles.
Similarly, the posterior condyle cuts are set to match the transepicondylar axis or 3° of
external rotation. Most current systems reference the posterior condyles rather than the
anterior cortex to match the anteroposterior height of the femoral component; however,

anterior referencing guides are available. Resection is intended to match the thickness of
the posterior condyles of the femoral component, which varies by manufacturer. As with
the distal femur cuts, which are set at 3° less than the anatomic distal femoral angle, the
posterior condyle cuts frequently are asymmetric because the distal femur cut is set
external to the posterior condyle axis. The lateral femoral condyle is not smaller than the
medial condyle. The cutting blocks simply are placed at an angle different from the
native anatomic axis of the femur, creating asymmetric bone cuts. The tibial cut is
independent of the femoral cuts and is intended to be set orthogonal to the anatomic
axis of the tibia in resecting an amount of bone equal to the thickness of the tibial tray
plus the thinnest liner available for that implant system. The rotation of the tibia is set to
match native tibial rotation (various methods), and the slope is orthogonal to the weight-
bearing axis in PCL-sacrificing designs or equal to the native slope if the PCL is retained.
In addition, because the native joint line is a mean of 3° in varus relative to the anatomic
tibial axis, the tibial cut also can create asymmetric tibial bone resections medial to
lateral. Soft-tissue balancing is then performed by releasing structures, such as
ligaments, tendons, and capsule, from the tight side to create rectangular gaps in flexion
and extension after the removal of osteophytes.
Balanced-gap techniques were designed to minimize the amount of soft-tissue releases
required while achieving overall mechanical alignment.4,5 The principle of the balanced-
gap technique involves tying the femoral component rotation to the tibial cut, thereby
achieving a balanced gap in flexion without the need for additional releases. The tibia is
cut first, after which femoral component rotation is set in flexion to be parallel to the
tibia with the collateral ligaments under equal tension. In patients with considerable
preoperative varus, surgeons may elect to cut the tibia with up to 3° of varus. If femoral
component rotation is set in flexion, rotation of the femoral cutting block will be closer
to its normal posterior condyle axis (ie, not externally rotated from its native rotation). By
setting femoral rotation to match the tibial cut, the balanced-gap technique results in
tissue balancing in flexion and extension with fewer releases than the traditional
mechanical alignment technique.
Kinematic Alignment

Kinematic alignment was developed after mechanical alignment and is designed to optimize
knee kinematics and address the painful TKA implant without compromising implant
survivorship.9
Dissimilar from the mechanical alignment and balanced-gap techniques, kinematic alignment
does not attempt to achieve mechanical alignment of the lower extremity but aims to restore
pre-arthritic knee alignment in the coronal, axial, and sagittal planes.
To achieve kinematic alignment, a caliper-based technique is used to resect only as much bone
as that replaced by the implant without altering the native three-dimensional shape or
position of the femur and tibia.
By matching native geometry, kinematic alignment results in a rectangular extension gap and
an asymmetric flexion gap.
Releasing the PCL would alter the flexion gap and potentially create flexion instability between
the femur and tibia.
Cruciate-retaining components are recommended for kinematic alignment techniques; no
research to date has been published on the results of kinematic alignment with the use of
posterior-stabilized implants.
Because the native nonarthritic knee is balanced, soft-tissue releases are not required to
balance the knee after the removal of osteophytes, except in the most extreme cases of
contracture.10
If the knee is not balanced in extension or flexion, the tibial bone cuts are revisited.
The literature on kinematic alignment includes an increasing number of studies assessing the
biomechanical and kinematic implications of the technique. Multiple studies have reported
equivalent or improved clinical results with no compromise of implant survivorship.4,10-12
Longer-term results are necessary because the technique was originally introduced in the
mid-2000s.

Kinematic Alignment
Kinematic alignment was developed after mechanical alignment and is designed to
optimize knee kinematics and address the painful TKA implant without compromising
implant survivorship.9 Dissimilar from the mechanical alignment and balanced-gap
techniques, kinematic alignment does not attempt to achieve mechanical alignment of
the lower extremity but aims to restore pre-arthritic knee alignment in the coronal, axial,

and sagittal planes regardless of alignment prior to the onset of arthritis. The rationale is
that the native soft-tissue envelope is, by definition, perfectly balanced if the bony
anatomy is reproduced. In addition, standing radiographs have documented that
kinematic alignment places the joint line parallel to the floor more effectively than
mechanical alignment techniques, thereby protecting the bone-cement interface from
harmful shearing forces.
Kinematic alignment is achieved a caliper-based technique, which aims to resect only as
much bone as that replaced by the implant without altering the native three-dimensional
shape or position of the femur and tibia. The surgeon measures the thickness of the
resected bone to ensure that equal amounts of bone and cartilage are resected from
both condyles, restoring the location and orientation of the joint line. Dissimilar from
mechanical alignment, kinematic alignment results in many final radiographic
alignments (HKA angles) that closely match the distribution of lower extremity alignment
in the normal, nonarthritic population, of which only 2% of the population has a perfect
mechanical axis.
Dissimilar from mechanical alignment, kinematic alignment matches native knee
geometry, creating a rectangular extension gap (the native knee has no play in full
extension/heel strike) and an asymmetric flexion gap (the native knee at 90° of flexion
has a wider lateral flexion gap to allow for rotation and roll back). The asymmetry may
vary from 2 to 5 mm and will match the native asymmetry of each patient.10,13
Therefore, the medial side re-creates the native medial pivot, whereas the lateral side
enables greater roll back in flexion. Releasing the PCL would alter the flexion gap,
potentially creating instability between the femur and tibia in flexion, just as it does in
the native knee. Therefore, cruciate-retaining components are recommended for
kinematic alignment techniques. No research to date has been published on the results
of kinematic alignment with the use of posterior-stabilized implants.
Because the native, nonarthritic knee is perfectly balanced, soft-tissue releases are not
required to balance the knee, except in the extreme cases of contractures.10 If the knee
is not balanced in extension, the tibial bone cuts are revisited. Instruments designed for
mechanical alignment can be used to achieve kinematic alignment; however, it may be a

challenge. Patient-specific instruments, robotics, and navigation have made kinematic
alignment easier.
The literature on kinematic alignment is quite robust, with a growing number of studies
assessing the biomechanical and kinematic implications of this alignment technique.
Multiple articles document excellent clinical results with no compromise of implant
survival, and compared with mechanical alignment, kinematic alignment results in equal
or improved functional scores, lower or similar strain in the tibial cortex, and lower
intraoperative contact pressures.5,10-12 Because kinematic alignment was introduced in
the mid-2000s, longer-term studies are necessary.
Kinematic Alignment and Competing Nomenclatures
Caliper-based alignment, restricted kinematic alignment (rKA), functional alignment, and
personalized arthroplasty
Caliper-based alignment is a newer term, equivalent to kinematic alignment.
rKA and functional alignment are techniques defined by the distance of the implants from
the neutral mechanical axis.14
Personalized arthroplasty is a relatively new technique that not only allows for patient-
specific anatomic variation but also accounts for other aspects unique to each patient (eg,
bone density; activity levels; disease type; and genomic, immunologic and rheumatologic
makeup) to determine the most suitable implant design and alignment and fixation
techniques.

Kinematic Alignment and Competing Nomenclatures
Other alignment strategies stemming from kinematic alignment include caliper-based
alignment, rKA, functional alignment, and personalized arthroplasty. Caliper-based
alignment is a relatively new term that often is used synonymously with kinematic
alignment. Caliper-based alignment is achieved intraoperatively by adjusting the bony
cuts for articular surface wear and measuring the thickness of the resected bone to
ensure that equal amounts of bone and cartilage are resected from both condyles,

thereby achieving unique native anatomic alignment in each patient. The distal femur
cut is based on the thickness of the normal cartilage of the distal femur, which varies but
is a mean of 2 mm. Therefore, the femoral cutting guide is positioned to resect an
amount of bone that is equal to the thickness of the implant, adjusting for lost cartilage
and bone resected by the saw. The bone fragment is measured with the use of a caliper
and should be 5 to 6 mm if the condyle was worn or 7 to 8 mm if the condyle was
unworn. For example, if the component is 8 mm, the total amount of bone, cartilage, and
saw kerf should equal 8 mm. Femoral rotation is based on the posterior condyle axis,
and adjustments are made for posterior lateral condyle wear in valgus knees. The bone
fragments should be 8 to 9 mm thick, adjusting for cartilage thickness. The tibial joint
line cut is set by resecting an equal amount of bone and cartilage from the medial and
lateral tibia and adjusting for any bone loss. The thickness of the resection should equal
the thickness of the tibial tray plus that of the smallest plastic insert for the system
under consideration. After completing resections and removing osteophytes, the
extension gap should be perfectly balanced while in flexion; the gap should be snug in
flexion and lax laterally by 2 to 5 mm, depending on the patient’s native anatomy, with
no necessary adjustments.
rKA and functional alignment are techniques defined by the distance of the implants
from the neutral mechanical axis.14 These techniques were developed because of
concerns that placing the tibial component in more than 3° of varus may lead to
mechanical complications; the techniques are a hybrid compromise between true
kinematic alignment and mechanical alignment.15 Proponents of kinematic alignment
have demonstrated that, in unrestricted kinematic alignment, the joint line is parallel to
the floor and orthogonal to the loading axis, which provides more physiologic loading in
knees that are aligned kinematically rather than mechanically. Therefore, proponents of
unrestricted kinematic alignment argue that no need to restrict alignment exists;
however, a paucity of data is available on rKA, no clear agreement exists on how much to
restrict varus on the tibial side, and no clear difference has been observed in outcomes
between rKA and kinematic alignment.
Personalized arthroplasty is a relatively new technique that not only allows for patient-
specific anatomic variation but also accounts for other aspects unique to each patient
(eg, bone density; activity levels; disease type; and genomic, immunologic and
